Question: Describe the current responsibilities of all three teams, and explain the org changes that produced this structure, step by step.
response_text:
**Current responsibilities of each team** | Team | Core responsibilities | Typical deliverables / activities | |------|-----------------------|-----------------------------------| | **Frontend Team** | • Design, develop, and maintain all client‑facing user interfaces (web, mobile‑web, native apps where applicable).
• Implement UI/UX specifications, ensure accessibility, and optimize performance for the end‑user experience.
• Own the component library, design system, and front‑end tooling (build pipelines, linting, testing frameworks).
• Work closely with product, design, and the Backend team to integrate APIs and deliver end‑to‑end features. | • React/Vue/Angular components, CSS/SCSS, Storybook UI library.
• Front‑end test suites (unit, integration, visual regression).
• CI/CD pipelines for front‑end artifacts.
• Performance monitoring (Lighthouse, Web Vitals). | | **Backend Team** | • Build and maintain the core business‑logic services, APIs, and data‑processing pipelines that power the product.
• Own the domain model, validation, authentication/authorization (business‑level), and integration with external services.
• Ensure API contracts are stable, versioned, and well‑documented (OpenAPI/GraphQL schemas).
• Write automated tests, handle error monitoring, and drive performance tuning of the service layer. | • Micro‑services, REST/GraphQL endpoints, background workers.
• Domain‑driven design, data‑access layers, transaction management.
• Service‑level testing, contract testing, load testing.
• API documentation portals. | | **Platform Team** (carved out of Backend) | • Own the underlying infrastructure, runtime environments, and platform services that host and run the Backend and Frontend code.
• Provide CI/CD pipelines, deployment automation, observability, scaling, and security hardening for the entire stack.
• Manage cloud resources (Kubernetes clusters, serverless platforms, databases, networking, IAM, secrets management).
• Offer self‑service platforms, internal tooling, and SLAs for reliability, availability, and cost‑optimization. | • IaC (Terraform, CloudFormation), Kubernetes manifests, Helm charts.
• CI/CD systems (GitHub Actions, Jenkins, Argo CD).
• Monitoring/alerting stacks (Prometheus, Grafana, Loki, Datadog).
• Service meshes, API gateways, secrets vaults, cost‑reporting dashboards. | --- ### Step‑by‑step evolution of the organization | Phase | Org structure | Reason for change | Resulting responsibilities | |-------|---------------|-------------------|----------------------------| | **Phase 1 – Single “Full‑Stack” team** (initial state) | • One team owned **both** front‑end and back‑end code, plus the infrastructure needed to run them. | • Early stage, small product scope, limited headcount.
• Simplicity: a single group could deliver end‑to‑end features quickly. | • Team members were “full‑stack” engineers, handling UI, API, and ops tasks. | | **Phase 2 – Split into Frontend & Backend** (as the company grew) | • Two distinct squads: **Frontend** and **Backend**.
• Both continued to manage their own runtime environments (e.g., the Backend team still provisioned servers, the Frontend team managed static‑site hosting). | • Product complexity increased; specialization allowed deeper expertise and faster delivery.
• Scaling headcount made it practical to have dedicated skill sets (UI/UX vs. domain logic). | • Frontend team took full ownership of the client‑side codebase and UI tooling.
• Backend team focused on business logic, APIs, and data services, while still handling the underlying infrastructure for those services. | | **Phase 3 – Platform team carved out of Backend** (need for dedicated infra focus) | • **Platform** team spun out from the Backend group.
• Backend team retained only **business‑logic** responsibilities; Platform took over **all infrastructure, CI/CD, observability, and reliability** concerns. | • The backend services grew in number, scale, and operational complexity (e.g., multiple micro‑services, multi‑region deployments).
• A dedicated group could standardize cloud usage, improve reliability, and free developers from “ops” distractions. | • Platform team now owns the cloud environment, deployment pipelines, monitoring, security, and cost‑management.
• Backend team concentrates on writing clean, testable business code and defining API contracts.
• Frontend team remains unchanged, continuing to own the UI layer. | | **Phase 4 – Current steady state** | • **Three** stable, cross‑functional teams: Frontend, Backend, Platform. | • The structure reflects a mature product with clear separation of concerns:
 • *What* the product does (Frontend & Backend) vs.
 • *How* it runs (Platform). | • Each team has a well‑defined charter, clear hand‑off points (e.g., Backend delivers API specs, Platform provides the deployment environment, Frontend consumes the APIs). | --- ### How the pieces fit together today 1. **Feature development flow** - **Product/Design** → **Frontend** (UI) & **Backend** (API) teams. - Backend publishes API contracts (OpenAPI/GraphQL). - Frontend consumes those contracts to build user‑facing features. 2. **Delivery pipeline** - Developers push code → **Platform** CI/CD pipelines build, test, and deploy to the shared cloud environment. - Platform enforces security policies, runs automated scans, and updates runtime configurations. 3. **Operations & reliability** - Platform monitors service health, scales resources, and handles incident response. - Backend and Frontend teams focus on fixing business‑logic bugs and UI defects, respectively, while Platform provides the observability data needed for debugging. 4. **Feedback loops** - Platform provides cost and performance metrics that inform Backend architectural decisions. - Frontend performance data (Web Vitals) feeds back into UI component optimizations. --- ### Summary - **Frontend Team** – owns everything the user interacts with, from UI components to client‑side tooling. - **Backend Team** – owns the domain‑centric services, APIs, and data handling, but no longer worries about the underlying infrastructure. - **Platform Team** – owns the cloud infrastructure, deployment automation, observability, security, and reliability engineering that enable the other two teams to ship code quickly and safely. The current three‑team structure emerged gradually: a single full‑stack group → split into Frontend & Backend → extraction of a dedicated Platform squad from Backend. Each step was driven by growth in product complexity, the need for deeper specialization, and the desire to separate *what* the system does from *how* it runs, resulting in clearer responsibilities, faster delivery cycles, and higher operational stability.
